The repeating stacking of the tubes and composite PCM was as follows: glycol serpentine – 35mm PCM slab – refrigerant serpentine – 35 mm PCM slab. The thermal network dictates that the heat flow from the glycol, through the composite PCM, and into the refrigerant. The prototype system design allowed for measured thermal performance of each of the sub- systems, and to discover the aspects that work well and those that require improvement. Given this, the system design was intended to provide the following functionality: 1. 17.6 kWth net cooling capacity at AHRAE standard conditions 2. > 1.2 hours of thermal energy storage 3. During full load hybrid mode, the TES should provide at least 1/3 of the peak cooling capacity throughout its discharge. This equates to delivering 10 °C chilled water at a discharge rate of ~ 6 kWth down to 10% SOC. 4. Efficient TES module charging is critical to overall energy use and utility costs. The TES was designed to maintain less than 5°C approach between refrigerant evaporator temperature and the TES module temperature at 17.6 kWt charge capacity. 6 This report is available at no cost from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) at www.nrel.gov/publications. The refrigeration cycle efficiency is sensitive to the saturated evaporator temperature; every 1 °C drop in evaporator temperature increases energy use by 0.03 kW/ton. A system with a seasonal energy efficiency rating (SEER) of 18 btu/Wh consumes 0.667 kW/ton seasonally (kW/ton = 12 / SEER). Thus a drop by 1°C in seasonally averaged evaporator temperature results in about 4.5% increase in seasonal energy. This penalty is inherent in an air conditioning system with a secondary fluid. Minimizing its effect is critical toward managing energy and power use. However, the thermal storage allows charging during cooler periods of the day, which can help mitigate this penalty. Task 2: Prototype characterization experiments Task Summary: Under this task, NET Energy and its OEM partners will fabricate prototypes of the PCM thermal storage modules and HVAC systems based on task-1 specifications and deliver them to NREL. NREL will characterize the performance of these prototypes in its laboratory, share these results with NET Energy and HVAC OEM, and use the results to validate or update their numerical models. NETenergy fabricated five thermal energy storage modules to be coupled with the charging and discharging sub-systems. The complete system was installed at the HVAC Laboratory at NREL for performance characterization. Figure 3 shows a schematic of the setup in the lab. Thermal energy storage modules (Figure 4) were connected to the refrigeration system (charging circuit) and the air-handling system coupled through a water-glycol loop (discharge circuit). We instrumented the refrigeration system, air-handling system, glycol circuit, and the thermal energy storage modules to measure various temperatures, pressures, flow rates in the system (Figure 5) to calculate heat transfer rates and characterize system performance.
